title: How a computer runs a program
summary: Follow one C program from source text to a running process: compiling and linking, the fetch-decode-execute loop, the stack, caches, system calls, scheduling and virtual memory.
outcomes: Explain what the preprocessor, compiler, assembler, linker and OS loader each do to turn source code into a process
Trace x86-64 assembly instruction by instruction, tracking registers and the program counter
Explain how call, ret and the stack pointer implement function calls, and why returning a pointer to a local is a bug
Compute average memory access time and predict which loop order is cache friendly
Explain how system calls, timer interrupts and page tables let the OS protect and share the machine

lessons.title: From hello.c to a running process

blocks.md: A CPU cannot read C. It only executes **machine code**: instructions encoded as bytes, sitting in memory. Running `./hello` therefore needs two separate jobs. First a **toolchain** translates your source text into an executable file of machine code. Later the **operating system** (OS) turns that file into a running **process**. This lesson walks the whole path once; the rest of the course zooms into each stage.

blocks.caption: The four stages GCC documents: preprocessing, compilation proper, assembly and linking, always in that order. Plain `gcc hello.c -o hello` runs all four.

blocks.md:
Each stage has one job:

- **Preprocessor**: pastes in `#include` files and expands macros. Output is still C text.
- **Compiler**: translates C into **assembly**, a human-readable text form of machine instructions for one CPU family (for example x86-64).
- **Assembler**: encodes each assembly instruction as bytes, producing an **object file** (`.o`).
- **Linker**: combines object files and libraries into one **executable**, filling in the addresses of functions defined elsewhere.

blocks.title: The path from source text to a process

scenes.caption: Everything starts as text you wrote. Nothing here can run yet.
The preprocessor expands #include and macros. The compiler then turns C into assembly for one CPU family, here x86-64.
The assembler encodes instructions as bytes. hello.o holds real machine code for main, but its library call (GCC turned this printf into puts) points at a symbol that is still undefined.
The linker combines hello.o with the C library, resolves puts, and writes an ELF executable: a file describing which bytes to place where in memory.
When you type ./hello, the shell calls execve. The kernel replaces the calling process's program with hello: new stack, heap and data segments, then jumps to its entry point.

blocks.prompt: `hello.o` already contains machine code for `main`. Why can't the OS run `hello.o` directly?
blocks.reveal: Because it is incomplete. Build it with `gcc` and run `objdump -t hello.o`: the call's target is listed as `*UND*` (undefined). It is named `puts`, not `printf`: GCC quietly replaces `printf` of a constant string ending in a newline with the cheaper `puts`, even at -O0. `objdump -r` shows a **relocation**: a note saying "patch the address of puts into these bytes later". Only the linker knows where `puts` will end up, so only the linked executable is runnable.

blocks.md: The executable on Linux uses the **ELF** format (described in `man 5 elf`). Besides the machine code (the `.text` section) and initialized global data (`.data`), it carries a **program header table** that tells the OS which parts of the file to map into memory, at which addresses, with which permissions. If the program uses shared libraries, ELF also names an **interpreter** (the dynamic loader, for glibc usually `ld-linux`) that execve uses to load those libraries.

Loading is not copying the whole file up front. As *Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces* (OSTEP) explains, modern OSes load lazily: they set up the mapping and bring in pieces of code or data only when they are first touched. The OS also creates the **stack**, puts `argc` and `argv` on it for `main`, sets up the standard input, output and error file descriptors, and finally transfers control to the program.

A **program** is a file of bytes on disk. A **process** is a running instance of it: its own memory (code, data, heap, stack), its own register values, and OS bookkeeping such as open files. One program can be running as many processes at once.

Misconception: "the compiler makes something the CPU runs straight off the disk." The CPU only fetches instructions from memory. An executable is inert until the OS loader maps it into a process's memory and points the CPU at its entry point.

blocks.question: You split a program into `main.c` and `util.c`. `main.c` calls `parse()` defined in `util.c`. Which stage is the first one that needs to see both files?
options: The preprocessor, because it must find parse()
The compiler, because it must check parse() exists
The assembler, because it encodes the call instruction
The linker, because it resolves the call to parse() across object files
blocks.explain: Each .c file is preprocessed, compiled and assembled on its own; a declaration of `parse` (usually from a header) is enough for the compiler. The call is left as an undefined symbol plus a relocation in main.o. The linker is the first stage that sees both object files and patches the real address in.

blocks.question: Which statement about running `./hello` is correct?
options: The shell reads hello's machine code and executes it itself
The kernel, via execve, replaces the current process image with hello and starts it at its entry point
The CPU loads the ELF file from disk one instruction at a time as it runs
The linker runs again every time you start the program
blocks.explain: execve(2): the program currently run by the calling process is replaced with a new one, with a newly initialized stack, heap and data segments. The CPU never reads from the disk file directly; pages of the file are mapped into memory and loaded when touched.

lessons.title: The CPU loop: fetch, decode, execute, repeat

blocks.md: Inside the CPU, the state a program can see is small: a handful of **registers** and the **program counter**. A register is a tiny, very fast storage slot inside the CPU; x86-64 has 16 general-purpose 64-bit registers (`rax`, `rbx`, `rcx`, `rdx`, `rsi`, `rdi`, `rbp`, `rsp`, `r8` to `r15`). The program counter, called `rip` on x86-64, holds the memory address of the next instruction.

The CPU then does one thing forever:

1. **Fetch** the instruction bytes at the address in the program counter.
2. **Decode** them: which operation, which registers or memory operands.
3. **Execute** it: compute, load from or store to memory, and update the program counter, either to the next instruction or to a jump target.

That is the whole model. Every loop, `if` and function call is built from it.

blocks.caption: A tiny function. We compile it with clang -O1 for x86-64 Linux and run it by hand.

blocks.md: Two conventions to read the trace. The assembly is in **AT&T syntax**: `addq %rcx, %rax` means "add rcx into rax" (source first, destination last). And the **System V x86-64 ABI** (the calling rules Linux uses) passes the first integer arguments in `rdi` and `rsi` and returns the result in `rax`. So `a` arrives in `rdi`, `n` in `rsi`, and the answer must end up in `rax`.

blocks.title: Stepping through sum(a, 3) instruction by instruction
blocks.code:
sum:
  testq %rsi, %rsi          # 0x00  is n <= 0?
  jle   .LBB0_1              # 0x03  if so, skip the loop
  xorl  %ecx, %ecx           # 0x05  i = 0
  xorl  %eax, %eax           # 0x07  s = 0
  nopl  (%rax)               # 0x09  padding, does nothing
.LBB0_4:
  addq  (%rdi,%rcx,8), %rax  # 0x10  s += a[i]
  incq  %rcx                 # 0x14  i++
  cmpq  %rcx, %rsi           # 0x17  compare n with i
  jne   .LBB0_4              # 0x1a  loop if i != n
  retq                       # 0x1c  return s (in rax)
.LBB0_1:
  xorl  %eax, %eax           # 0x1d  return 0
  retq                       # 0x1f

scenes.caption: Called as sum(a, 3) with a at address 0x1000 holding 3, 1, 4. The ABI put a in rdi and n in rsi. testq computes n AND n and records whether the result is zero or negative in the CPU's flags, which the next jump reads.
n is 3, so the conditional jump is not taken. The CPU simply moves on: rip advances past this 2-byte instruction to 0x05.
Two xorl instructions zero i (rcx) and s (rax). XOR of a register with itself is 0; writing a 32-bit register also clears its upper 32 bits.
First trip through the loop. addq computes the address rdi + 8 x rcx = 0x1000, loads 3 from memory, and adds it to rax.
incq makes i = 1, cmpq compares n with i, and jne sees they differ, so it writes 0x10 into rip. That jump is the whole loop.
Second trip: address 0x1000 + 8 x 1 = 0x1008 holds 1, so s becomes 4.
Third trip: address 0x1010 holds 4, so s becomes 8.
Now i = 3 equals n, so jne is not taken and execution falls through to retq.
retq returns to the caller with the answer 8 in rax. In total the CPU executed 18 instructions: 5 before the loop, 4 per element, and 1 return.

blocks.md: Each line above is stored as bytes. Disassembling the object file with `objdump -d` shows them; instructions on x86-64 vary in length, so the program counter advances by a different amount each time.

blocks.code:
10: 48 03 04 cf     addq  (%rdi,%rcx,8), %rax
  14: 48 ff c1        incq  %rcx
  17: 48 39 ce        cmpq  %rcx, %rsi
  1a: 75 f4           jne   0x10
  1c: c3              retq
blocks.caption: The loop body as machine code (offsets in hex). 4 + 3 + 3 + 2 bytes, then a 1-byte return.

blocks.prompt: The jump `jne` is encoded as just two bytes, `75 f4`. The byte `f4` is the signed number -12. Where does it send the CPU?
blocks.reveal: To **0x10**, the top of the loop. By the time the jump executes, the program counter already points at the next instruction, 0x1c. A taken jump adds the offset: 0x1c - 12 = 0x10. There is no special loop hardware: a jump is just an instruction that writes a new value into the program counter.

blocks.md: Control flow is the program counter. Straight-line code advances it by the instruction length; `jmp`, conditional jumps, `call` and `ret` overwrite it. A C `for` loop compiles to a compare plus a conditional jump backwards.

Simplified: real CPUs pipeline and overlap many instructions, and even execute them out of order. But they are built so that the visible result is exactly as if each instruction ran one at a time in program order, which is why this model is the right one to reason with.

blocks.question: Using the same compiled code, how many instructions does the CPU execute for sum(a, 1000)?
blocks.explain: 5 instructions run once before the loop (test, jle, two xors, the padding nop), the 4-instruction loop body runs 1000 times, and retq runs once: 5 + 4000 + 1 = 4006. Instruction count grows with n because the loop body is re-fetched and re-executed each iteration.

blocks.question: In `addq (%rdi,%rcx,8), %rax`, why is rcx multiplied by 8?
options: Because x86-64 has 8 general-purpose registers
Because each long is 8 bytes, so element i starts 8 x i bytes after a
Because the loop is unrolled 8 times
Because memory is read in 8-bit units
blocks.explain: Memory is addressed in bytes, and a long is 8 bytes on x86-64 Linux. a[i] therefore lives at address a + 8 x i. The CPU computes that address as part of the instruction (base rdi plus index rcx times scale 8).

lessons.title: Where a program's memory lives: code, heap and stack

blocks.md: Every process gets an **address space**: the range of memory addresses it can use, which looks to the program like one long array of bytes. OSTEP's model divides it into three parts. The **code** (the program's instructions) and static data sit at fixed places. The **heap** holds memory requested at run time with `malloc` and released with `free`. The **stack** holds local variables, saved registers and return addresses for function calls.

scenes.caption: Code and static data come straight from the executable file; their size is known before the program starts.
The heap grows toward higher addresses as malloc asks the OS for more memory. Heap memory lives until free is called.
The stack starts high and grows toward lower addresses with each call. A frame disappears as soon as its function returns.
Simplified: real layouts also include shared libraries, memory-mapped files and randomized start addresses. The big gap lets both heap and stack grow.

blocks.md: The stack is managed with one register, `rsp`, the **stack pointer**, which holds the address of the top of the stack. On x86-64 the stack grows toward lower addresses: `push` subtracts 8 from `rsp` and stores a value there; `pop` loads it and adds 8 back. A function call is just two instructions: `call f` pushes the **return address** (the address of the instruction after the call) and jumps to `f`; `ret` pops that address into the program counter.

blocks.code:
__attribute__((noinline)) long square(long x) { return x * x; }
long sumsq(long a, long b) { return square(a) + square(b); }

# clang -O1, x86-64 Linux
square:                    sumsq:
  movq  %rdi, %rax           pushq %r14
  imulq %rdi, %rax           pushq %rbx
  retq                       pushq %rax       # 8 bytes of padding
                             movq  %rsi, %rbx
                             callq square
                             movq  %rax, %r14
                             movq  %rbx, %rdi
                             callq square
                             addq  %r14, %rax
                             addq  $8, %rsp   # drop the padding
                             popq  %rbx
                             popq  %r14
                             retq
blocks.caption: Real compiler output. noinline stops clang from merging square into sumsq so we can watch the calls.

scenes.caption: main has just executed call sumsq. The call pushed the return address into main (ret:m), so rsp = S. Arguments arrived in registers: rdi = 3, rsi = 4.
sumsq saves r14 and rbx, which the ABI says a function must preserve for its caller, then pushes rax only as 8 bytes of padding so rsp is a multiple of 16 at the next call, as the ABI requires.
b = 4 is copied into rbx, then call square pushes the return address into sumsq (ret:s) and jumps. rsp = S-32.
square computes 3 x 3 = 9 in rax and executes ret, which pops ret:s into the program counter. Back in sumsq, 9 is stashed in r14.
The second call reuses the very same slot: push ret:s, square(4) returns 16, pop. addq then makes rax = 9 + 16 = 25.
sumsq drops the padding, restores rbx and r14, and ret pops ret:m. The stack is exactly as main left it, and the result 25 is in rax.

blocks.prompt: A buggy function copies 40 bytes of user input into a 16-byte local array on the stack. What can go wrong when the function executes `ret`?
blocks.reveal: The extra bytes overwrite whatever lies above the array in the frame, which can include saved registers and the **return address**. `ret` blindly pops that slot into the program counter, so the CPU jumps wherever the input bytes say: usually a crash, and in the classic **stack buffer overflow** attack, code of the attacker's choosing. The CPU has no idea the value was not written by `call`.

blocks.md: `call` = push return address + jump. `ret` = pop into the program counter. Everything a function keeps on the stack lives only until it returns, which is why the stack can be reused so cheaply.

Never return a pointer to a local variable. Its stack slot is reused by the very next call (as the second call to square reused the first one's slot), so the pointer soon points at unrelated data. Use the heap (malloc) for data that must outlive the function.

blocks.question: Why does sumsq copy b into rbx before calling square, instead of leaving it in rsi?
options: Because rsi is reserved for return values
Because square may overwrite rsi freely, while the ABI requires square to preserve rbx
Because rbx is faster than rsi
Because the stack is full
blocks.explain: The System V ABI splits registers into caller-saved ones (like rdi, rsi, rax) that any callee may clobber, and callee-saved ones (rbx, rbp, r12 to r15) that a callee must restore before returning. That is also why sumsq itself pushes rbx and r14 first: it is about to use them and must hand them back intact.

blocks.question: Right after `call square` executes, which statement is true?
options: rsp increased by 8 and the program counter points at square
rsp decreased by 8, the stack top holds the address of the instruction after the call, and the program counter points at square
rsp is unchanged; the return address is kept in a special register
rsp decreased by 8 and the stack top holds the address of square
blocks.explain: The stack grows down, so a push subtracts 8 from rsp. call pushes the return address (the next instruction in the caller), not the target, then jumps by writing square's address into the program counter.

lessons.title: Why memory is slow and how caches hide it

blocks.md: So far each `addq` that read memory looked as cheap as one that only touched registers. It is not. Main memory (DRAM) sits off the CPU chip and takes far longer to answer than the CPU takes to execute an instruction. To hide that gap, CPUs keep copies of recently used memory in small, fast on-chip memories called **caches**, organized in levels: L1 is smallest and fastest, then L2, and often L3.

blocks.title: Cost of one access, in CPU cycles (Intel Pentium M)

scenes.caption: Ulrich Drepper's memory paper lists Intel's numbers for the Pentium M: about 3 cycles for L1d, 14 for L2, 240 for main memory. Newer CPUs differ, but the gap of roughly two orders of magnitude remains.
One trip to main memory costs as much time as 80 L1 hits. A program that misses the cache often spends most of its time waiting, not computing.

blocks.md: Caches do not store single bytes. They move fixed-size blocks called **cache lines**, and as Drepper notes, 64 bytes is now the norm. A miss on one byte brings in its 63 neighbours too. This works because programs show **locality** (OSTEP's terms): **temporal** locality (data used recently is likely used again soon, like a loop counter) and **spatial** locality (data near a recent access is likely next, like the next array element).

C stores a 2D array in **row-major** order: `a[i][j]` and `a[i][j+1]` are neighbours, while `a[i+1][j]` is a whole row away. Take a tiny 4 by 8 array of 8-byte longs, so each row fills exactly one 64-byte line, and a toy cache that holds only 2 lines and evicts the least recently used one. Summing it row by row and column by column does the same additions, but not the same memory traffic.

blocks.title: Hits and misses: row order vs column order

scenes.caption: Row-by-row order. The first access a[0][0] misses: the cache fetches the whole 64-byte line, which is all 8 longs of row 0.
The other 7 elements of row 0 are already in that line: 7 hits. This is spatial locality paying off.
After the whole array: 4 misses and 28 hits. One miss per line, no matter how small the cache.
Column-by-column order with the same 2-line cache. a[0][0], a[1][0], a[2][0], a[3][0] are in 4 different lines: 4 misses, and the first two lines are already evicted.
Moving to column 1, a[0][1] needs row 0's line again, but it was evicted. Every access misses.
After the whole array: 32 misses out of 32. Same data, same additions, 8x the misses, purely from access order.

blocks.prompt: Scale up: a 1024 by 1024 array of longs (8 MiB) and a 32 KiB cache (512 lines, fully associative, LRU). What fraction of accesses miss when summing row by row, and column by column?
blocks.reveal: Simulated: row order misses **12.5%** (one miss per 8 longs), column order misses **100%**. Column order jumps 8 KiB between accesses, so each one lands in a new line, and by the time the loop returns to a line, 1023 other lines have pushed it out of the 512-line cache.

blocks.tex: \text{average access time} = t_{\text{hit}} + (\text{miss rate}) \times t_{\text{miss penalty}}
blocks.caption: A simple one-level cache model: every access pays the hit time, and misses also pay the trip to memory.

blocks.md: Plug in the Pentium M numbers ($t_\text{hit} = 3$, penalty $= 240$ cycles). Row order: $3 + 0.125 \times 240 = 33$ cycles per access. Column order: $3 + 1 \times 240 = 243$ cycles, about 7.4x slower for identical arithmetic.

blocks.title: Average access time vs miss rate

scenes.caption: With a 240-cycle penalty, the line is steep: every extra percent of misses adds 2.4 cycles to the average access.
If misses only go to L2 (Drepper's L2 takes about 14 cycles, so roughly 11 more than an L1 hit), even a high miss rate is tolerable. The two points still mark the 240-cycle case.

blocks.md: Simplified model. Real CPUs have several cache levels, and **hardware prefetchers** detect sequential and strided access and fetch lines before they are asked for, hiding much of the cost of row order (and some of column order). Measured slowdowns vary by machine; the direction does not.
Performance is often decided by memory access patterns, not instruction counts. Touch memory sequentially, reuse data while it is still in cache, and keep hot data small.

blocks.question: A colleague's loop `for j: for i: total += m[i][j]` over a large C 2D array of longs is slow. What is the most effective first fix?
options: Swap the loops so the inner loop walks j along a row
Use a faster add instruction
Make total a global variable
Add more threads before changing anything
blocks.explain: In C, m[i][j] and m[i][j+1] are adjacent, so walking j in the inner loop uses all 8 longs of every 64-byte line it fetches. The current inner loop strides a full row per access, fetching a new line every time.

blocks.question: With a 3-cycle hit time and a 240-cycle miss penalty, what is the average access time at a 5% miss rate?
options: 12 cycles
15 cycles
243 cycles
8 cycles
blocks.explain: 3 + 0.05 x 240 = 3 + 12 = 15 cycles. Note that a 5% miss rate already makes the average access 5x slower than a hit: misses dominate.

lessons.title: The OS in charge: system calls and sharing the CPU

blocks.md: Two problems remain. A program must not be able to read another program's files or drive the disk directly, yet it needs to do I/O. And one program must not be able to hog the CPU forever. OSTEP calls the solution **limited direct execution**: the program runs directly on the CPU at full speed, but in a restricted processor mode.

The CPU has at least two modes. In **user mode**, privileged operations such as issuing I/O or reconfiguring the hardware are refused: attempting one raises an exception and the OS takes over. In **kernel mode**, where the OS runs, everything is allowed. A program asks the OS for a service with a **system call**: a special **trap** instruction that switches to kernel mode and jumps to a handler the kernel registered at boot in a **trap table**. A **return-from-trap** instruction later drops back to user mode.

On x86-64 Linux, the `syscall(2)` man page gives the exact rules: the trap instruction is `syscall`, the system call number goes in `rax`, arguments go in `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `r10`, `r8`, `r9`, and the result comes back in `rax`. The kernel's table lists `write` as number 1. So `printf` eventually becomes a `write(1, buf, len)` call, where 1 is standard output.

scenes.caption: An ordinary function call into the C library's write wrapper. Still user mode, no OS involved yet.
The wrapper puts 1 (the number for write) in rax and the arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, then executes the syscall instruction. The CPU switches to kernel mode and jumps to the kernel's entry point.
The kernel checks that file descriptor 1 is open and that buf is memory this process may read, then hands the 3 bytes to the terminal's driver.
Return-from-trap: back to user mode with the result, 3 bytes written, in rax. The wrapper returns it as an ordinary function result.

blocks.md: System calls give the OS control when a program asks. But what if it never asks, say it is stuck in `while (1) {}`? The answer, per OSTEP, is a **timer interrupt**: a hardware timer is programmed to interrupt the CPU every so many milliseconds. Each interrupt forcibly runs an OS handler, so the OS regains control no matter what the program does.

Once in control, the OS **scheduler** may decide to run a different process. It performs a **context switch**: it saves the current process's registers, including the program counter and stack pointer, into that process's kernel data, then restores another process's saved registers. When the return-from-trap executes, the CPU resumes the other process exactly where it was interrupted.

scenes.caption: Simplified model: each process gets a 10 ms time slice, after which the timer interrupts, and kernel work takes 1 ms (exaggerated so it is visible). Process A runs on the CPU directly, in user mode.
The timer interrupt fires. The kernel saves A's registers and restores B's: a context switch.
B runs until the next timer interrupt, then the kernel switches back. A resumes at the exact instruction it was on and cannot tell it was paused.
At 27 ms A calls read() on a file whose data must come from disk. A cannot continue until it arrives, so the kernel marks A blocked and runs B instead of letting the CPU sit idle.

blocks.prompt: A process runs `while (1) {}` and never makes a system call. On a single-core machine, can it freeze everything else?
blocks.reveal: No. The timer interrupt fires regardless of what user code is doing, the kernel's handler runs, and the scheduler can switch to other processes. The loop only burns its own time slices. And the process cannot turn the timer off: reprogramming it is a privileged operation, refused in user mode.

blocks.md: The OS is not running alongside your program; it runs only when something hands it the CPU: a system call (the program asks), an exception (the program did something illegal), or an interrupt (hardware such as the timer or the disk demands attention).

blocks.question: Which of these operations has to go through a system call?
options: Adding two numbers in registers
Calling a function defined in your own program
Reading bytes from a file
Writing to a local variable on the stack
blocks.explain: Arithmetic, function calls and stack accesses are ordinary user-mode instructions on the process's own memory. A file lives on a device that only the kernel may touch, so read() must trap into the kernel.

blocks.question: Why does a system call use a trap instruction instead of letting the program jump directly to the kernel's code for write?
options: Jumps cannot reach addresses that large
The trap switches to kernel mode and enters only at handlers the kernel registered, so a program cannot run arbitrary kernel code with full privileges
Trap instructions are faster than jumps
The C library has no way to call functions
blocks.explain: If user code could jump anywhere into the kernel with privileges, it could skip permission checks. The trap table, set up at boot in kernel mode, fixes the only entry points, and the mode switch happens in hardware as part of the trap.

lessons.title: Virtual memory: every process gets its own addresses

blocks.md: Two processes can use the very same address, say for a global variable, and still each hold a different value there. That works because addresses a program uses are **virtual**. On every memory access, hardware in the CPU, the **memory management unit** (MMU), translates the virtual address into a **physical** address in RAM, using a table the OS maintains separately for each process.

With **paging**, memory is cut into fixed-size **pages** (virtual) and **frames** (physical) of the same size. A virtual address splits into a **virtual page number** (VPN), its high bits, and an **offset** within the page, its low bits. The per-process **page table** maps each VPN to a physical frame number (PFN). The offset is not translated: it only says which byte within the page.

OSTEP's tiny example: a 64-byte address space with 16-byte pages, so 4 pages, a 2-bit VPN and a 4-bit offset. Its page table maps virtual page 0 to frame 3, page 1 to frame 7, page 2 to frame 5 and page 3 to frame 2. The program loads from virtual address 21.

scenes.caption: 21 in binary is 010101. Nothing is translated yet.
16-byte pages need 4 offset bits (2^4 = 16), leaving the top 2 bits as the VPN: 01, virtual page 1. The offset 0101 is byte 5 within that page.
The MMU indexes the page table with VPN 1 and finds physical frame 7.
Replace the VPN with the PFN, keep the offset: 111 then 0101 gives 1110101, physical address 117. The load reads RAM byte 117.

blocks.md: Real x86-64 numbers. Pages are 4 KiB, so the offset is 12 bits ($2^{12} = 4096$). With 4-level paging, virtual addresses use 48 bits; Linux's documented memory map gives user space the lower half, 128 TB. A single flat table for the remaining 36 bits would be huge, so the page table is a tree of 4 levels. Each table node is one 4 KiB page of 8-byte entries, which is 512 entries, so each level consumes 9 bits: $4 \times 9 + 12 = 48$.

scenes.caption: A typical user-space stack address. The low 48 bits are split into four 9-bit table indices and a 12-bit offset.
Computed with shifts and masks: indices 255, 500, 145, 325. Each picks one of 512 entries in a table, whose entry points to the next level's table.
The last-level entry gives the physical frame; the offset 0x678 (byte 1656) is copied through unchanged. A full walk costs up to 4 extra memory reads.

blocks.md: Four extra memory reads per access would be ruinous, given lesson 4. So the MMU caches recent translations in a **translation lookaside buffer** (TLB), which OSTEP describes as a hardware cache of popular virtual-to-physical translations. Thanks to locality, most accesses hit in the TLB and skip the walk entirely. Page-table entries also carry a **present bit**: if a page is not in memory, the access raises a **page fault**, the OS runs, loads or allocates the page, and the instruction is retried. That is how the lazy loading from lesson 1 works.

blocks.prompt: Process A and process B both store a value at virtual address 0x7ffd12345678. Does B overwrite A's value?
blocks.reveal: No. Each process has its own page table, so the same virtual page maps to different physical frames. Neither process can even name the other's memory, since every address it can produce goes through its own table. This isolation is the foundation of process protection, and the OS switches page tables as part of every context switch between processes.

blocks.md: Every address your program uses is virtual. The MMU translates it on every access using the current process's page table, the TLB makes that fast, and page faults let the OS fill in memory lazily.

blocks.question: With 4 KiB pages, what is the offset within its page of virtual address 0x7ffd12345678?
blocks.explain: 4 KiB = 2^12 bytes, so the offset is the low 12 bits, which is the last 3 hex digits: 0x678. The remaining bits select the page through the 4-level table.

blocks.question: Why does x86-64 use a 4-level tree instead of one flat table indexed by the 36-bit page number?
options: A flat table would need 2^36 entries x 8 bytes = 512 GiB per process, mostly describing unused memory
A flat table cannot be cached in the TLB
Flat tables cannot hold physical frame numbers
Hardware cannot index arrays larger than 512 entries
blocks.explain: 2^36 x 8 bytes = 512 GiB, for every process. A tree only allocates the lower-level tables for regions actually in use, so a small process needs a few pages of page tables. The cost is the longer walk, which the TLB hides.
